target: De haber tenido tiempo, habría ido a visitarte.
english: Had I had time, I would have gone to visit you.
tip: Spanish can shrink a whole if-clause into two words: de + infinitive. De haber tenido tiempo = 'if I had had time' – no si, no subject, and very common in writing.

target: No me tomes el pelo; sé que no es verdad.
english: Don't pull my leg – i know it's not true.
tip: Where English pulls legs, Spanish grabs hair: no me tomes el pelo = 'don't take my hair', i.e. stop teasing me. Same joke, different body part.

target: De tal palo, tal astilla; el hijo es identico al padre.
english: Like father, like son – the son is identical to the father.
tip: De tal palo, tal astilla is carpentry: a splinter (astilla) carved off a stick (palo) is the same wood – just as el hijo is cut from el padre.

target: ¿Necesitaremos una canguro para el sábado?
english: Will we need a babysitter for Saturday?
tip: Una canguro is literally 'a kangaroo' – Spain's everyday word for a babysitter. Latin America uses niñera instead.

target: Saldremos temprano para evitar el tráfico.
english: We will leave early to avoid traffic.
tip: Why saldremos, not saliremos? The future squeezed out salir's i, and the leftover salr- was awkward – so Spanish wedged in a d as a bridge: sal-d-remos.

target: No podremos terminar el proyecto a tiempo.
english: We will not be able to finish the project on time.
tip: Podremos isn't poder + emos: the future drops poder's e, leaving podr-. Saber and haber do the same – sabr-, habr-.

target: Pase lo que pase, siempre seré tu madre.
english: Whatever happens, I'll always be your mother.
tip: Pase lo que pase is literally 'may it happen what may happen'. The doubled subjunctive means 'no matter what' – the statement holds whatever the outcome.

target: Mi hermano y yo nos peleábamos de pequeños.
english: My brother and I used to fight as kids.
tip: Imperfect for habitual past: nos peleábamos = we used to fight.

target: Según él, el proyecto estaría listo para el viernes.
english: According to him, the project would be ready by Friday.
tip: Estaría here isn't polite 'would be' – with según él it's the reporting conditional: 'is supposedly ready'. Spanish news uses it to flag unconfirmed claims.

target: La catedral fue construida en el siglo quince.
english: The cathedral was built in the fifteenth century.
tip: Spanish centuries skip 'fifteenth': el siglo quince is literally 'century fifteen'. Past the tenth century, ordinals get clunky, so plain numbers take over.

target: Cuanto antes lo terminemos, mejor será para todos.
english: The sooner we finish it, the better it will be for everyone.
tip: English needs two 'the's (the sooner, the better); Spanish drops both: cuanto antes lo terminemos, mejor – and the not-yet-done verb goes subjunctive (terminemos).

target: Se oyen risas desde la habitación de los niños.
english: You can hear laughter from the kids' room.
tip: Se oyen is plural because risas is the grammatical subject – literally 'laughters hear themselves'. With this se, the thing heard controls the verb: se oye un ruido, se oyen risas.

target: Necesitamos a alguien que domine las hojas de calculo.
english: We need someone who can handle spreadsheets.
tip: Domine is subjunctive because this spreadsheet wizard may not exist yet – alguien que + subjunctive describes a wish list, not a real person you've already found.

target: El profesor cuyas clases más me gustaban se jubiló.
english: The teacher whose classes I liked the most retired.
tip: "Cuyas" = whose (f. pl.): Cuyo agrees in gender/number with the noun it precedes, not the owner.

target: El destino no es cuestión de suerte, sino de decisión.
english: Destiny is not a matter of luck, but of decision.
tip: Two 'buts' in Spanish: after a negation that corrects, pero gives way to sino – no es cuestión de suerte, sino de decisión ('not X but rather Y').

target: Haré lo que sea necesario.
english: I'll do whatever is necessary.
tip: Why sea, not es? Unknown things get subjunctive: 'lo que sea necesario' = whatever turns out to be necessary. 'Lo que es' would mean you already know what that is.

target: No sé qué habrá pasado.
english: I don't know what could have happened.
tip: Future perfect for past speculation: "¿Qué habrá pasado?" (What could have happened?). Guessing about past events.

target: Vamos a caminar por el parque.
english: We're going to walk through the park.
tip: 'For the park'? No – 'por el parque' means through/around it. Por marks movement inside a space: caminar por = wander through, not walk for.

target: Nos veremos la semana que viene.
english: We'll see each other next week.
tip: Where's 'each other'? Packed into nos: 'nos veremos' = we'll see each other. Spanish reciprocals ride the same pronouns as reflexives – context decides which.

target: Vamos a pedir un aumento de sueldo.
english: Let's ask for a raise.
tip: Don't add 'for' – pedir already means ask FOR: 'pedir un aumento' = ask for a raise. 'Pedir por' exists, but it means to plead on someone's behalf.

target: Los primos con los que jugábamos viven lejos.
english: The cousins we used to play with live far away.
tip: English strands prepositions ('cousins we played with'); Spanish never does. Con jumps up front: 'los primos con los que jugábamos' – preposition + article + que.

target: Si hubiera hecho la reserva, tendríamos mesa ahora.
english: If I had made the reservation, we would have a table now.
tip: 'hubiera hecho' (past condition) + 'tendríamos' (present result) = a mixed conditional.

target: Con tal de que seas feliz, yo estaré bien.
english: As long as you're happy, I'll be fine.
tip: 'Con tal de que' is literally 'with such (a condition) that' = as long as. It names a condition, so subjunctive follows: con tal de que seas feliz.

target: No tiene ni pies ni cabeza lo que estas diciendo.
english: What you're saying makes no sense.
tip: Ni pies ni cabeza is literally 'neither feet nor head' = it makes no sense. Where English can't make head or tail of something, Spanish says it's missing both ends.

target: Antes de salir compruebo que todas las ventanas están cerradas.
english: Before leaving I check that all the windows are closed.
tip: Why están, not son? Closed is the windows' current state – the result of someone shutting them. Estar + participle = resulting condition: 'están cerradas'.

target: Llovía mucho cuando llegamos.
english: It was raining a lot when we arrived.
tip: Two pasts, one line: llovía (imperfect) sets the ongoing background; llegamos (preterite) is the completed event that happened against it.

target: Seguro que ya lo habrás oído.
english: I'm sure you'll have heard of it already.
tip: Habrás oído looks future but aims backward: with seguro que ya, it's a confident bet about the past – 'you'll have heard it' meaning 'I'm sure you already have.'

target: Creo que lloverá este fin de semana.
english: I think it'll rain this weekend.
tip: No subjunctive after 'creo que'! Affirmative belief asserts something real: creo que lloverá. Only the negative flips it: no creo que llueva.

target: Es mediodía y todavía no he comido.
english: It's noon and I still haven't eaten.
tip: Spanish has no word for 'yet' – it recycles 'still': 'todavía no he comido' is literally 'still I haven't eaten' = I haven't eaten yet.

target: Lo haré en cuanto tenga un momento.
english: I'll do it as soon as I have a moment.
tip: En cuanto + subjunctive for future events: tenga (not tengo).
